questions.prompt: Put these steps of building and running a new report, per the Report Builder lesson, in the correct order.
items: From the Reports tab, click New Report and choose a report type
Drag fields from the Fields pane into the Outline tab's Groups and Columns
Switch to the Filters tab and narrow down which records show up
Click Save, giving the report a clear name and a folder
Click Save & Run to execute the report against the full data set
questions.explain: The Report Builder always runs in this order: pick the report type first (since it decides what fields even exist to drag), build the Outline, narrow with Filters, save with a real name and folder, then run against the full data. The live preview shown while building is only a partial result — Save & Run is what replaces it with the real thing.

questions.prompt: An admin needs a report listing every Account that has never had a single Opportunity created against it. Which report-type relationship setting makes this possible, and why would the other option fail?
options: "Accounts with or without Opportunities" — because the more restrictive "with" option would behave like an inner join and drop every account that has zero matching opportunities
"Accounts with Opportunities" — because it includes every account regardless of whether a matching opportunity exists
Either setting works identically, since the report's filters decide which accounts show up, not the relationship setting
Neither setting can do this; a cross filter is required instead and the relationship choice is irrelevant
questions.explain: "A with or without B" behaves like a left join — every primary record (every Account) shows up whether or not a related Opportunity exists, with Opportunity fields simply blank where there's no match. "A with B" behaves like an inner join and silently removes exactly the accounts-with-zero-opportunities rows this report needs.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the moment you drag a field into Group Rows, the Outline tab automatically changes a report's format from Tabular to a ________ report, complete with subtotals for every group.
questions.explain: Grouping is what makes a report a summary report in Lightning Experience — you don't choose the Summary format first and group second. The instant a field lands in Group Rows, the report gains subtotals and its format switches automatically.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about matrix reports.
options: A matrix report groups by both rows and columns at the same time, forming a true two-dimensional grid
Every cell in the grid is the intersection of one row group and one column group
A matrix report can only use Sum as its summary type — Average, Count, Max, and Min aren't available
A single grand total sits in the bottom-right corner, the intersection of every row and every column
Adding a second field to Group Rows alone (with nothing in Group Columns) is what turns a summary report into a matrix report
questions.explain: A matrix report groups rows and columns simultaneously, and each cell is the summarized intersection of one row group and one column group, with a single grand total in the bottom-right corner. Any of the standard summary types (Sum, Average, Max, Min, Count) can be used, not just Sum. Stacking a second field into Group Rows only produces nested row groups inside a summary report — a matrix requires a field in Group Columns specifically.

questions.prompt: A sales manager wants three separate views — Closed Opportunities, Open Pipeline, and Win Rate & Projection — lined up side by side, all grouped by the same Opportunity Owner so the numbers compare directly. Which report format and feature combination fits?
options: A Joined report with each view as its own block, using Group Across Blocks on Opportunity Owner
A single Matrix report with Opportunity Owner in Group Rows and the three views stacked in Group Columns
Three separate Tabular reports exported individually and merged afterward in a spreadsheet
A Summary report with three nested row-level formulas, one for each view
questions.explain: A joined report is exactly for comparisons that span more than one report type or filtered slice — each view becomes its own block (up to five total), and Group Across Blocks applies one shared row grouping, like Opportunity Owner, so every block's numbers line up against the same rows.

questions.prompt: Match each part of the Lightning Report Builder to what it actually does.
right: Narrows down which records show up in the results
A live but partial view of the report while you're still building it
Lists every field the chosen report type exposes, organized by object
Where fields get dragged into Groups and Columns
questions.explain: The Fields pane lists every field the report type exposes. The Outline tab is where you drag fields into Groups and Columns. The Filters tab narrows down which records appear. The Preview pane shows a live, partial preview — not the complete result set — while you're still editing.

questions.prompt: A report builder wants to add both a row-level formula and several summary formulas to the same report. Per the Formulas in Reports lesson, what are the correct maximums?
options: Up to one row-level formula and up to five summary formulas
Up to one row-level formula and up to one summary formula
Up to five row-level formulas and up to five summary formulas
Up to five row-level formulas and up to one summary formula
Unlimited row-level formulas, but only one summary formula allowed per group
There is no fixed limit on either type of formula
questions.explain: A report can hold at most one row-level formula, which calculates a value per record, and up to five summary formulas, each calculating a value per group or for the whole report. Those are the two separate caps the lesson gives.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B gets the row-level formula limit right but wrong on summary formulas — a report can actually hold up to five summary formulas, not just one, which is exactly what lets you build a win rate and a percent-of-total column side by side in the same report.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: inside a report grouped by Year and then by Month, a summary formula that calculates each month's percent of its year's total would use the ________ function to reach the outer grouping level.
questions.explain: PARENTGROUPVAL returns a summarized value from an outer (parent) grouping level — exactly what's needed to compare a month's value against the total for the year it sits inside. PREVGROUPVAL, by contrast, reaches the previous group at the same level, which is the tool for a month-over-month change column instead.

questions.prompt: An admin needs a report of Accounts that have zero related Contact records. Why is a cross filter the right tool here instead of a field-to-field filter?
options: A field-to-field filter compares two fields on the same record; it can't test whether a related record exists at all — only a cross filter's with/without logic answers that
A field-to-field filter is simply a faster version of a cross filter and either one works identically here
A cross filter can only be used on currency fields, so it's the only option for counting related records
A field-to-field filter would work fine, but only if the Contact field is renamed to match the Account field first
questions.explain: A field-to-field filter compares one field on a record to another field on that same record — useful for something like Actual Cost vs. Budgeted Cost, but it has no concept of a related object existing or not. A cross filter is built specifically for "has a related record" vs. "doesn't," using a with/without operator against a secondary object — exactly what "Accounts without Contacts" needs.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about bucket columns.
options: A single report can have up to five bucket columns, each holding up to twenty buckets
A bucket column lives entirely inside one report — it doesn't create a new field on the object or affect any other report
A source value not assigned to any bucket causes the report to throw an error and fail to run
A bucket column behaves like any other column afterward — it can be sorted, filtered, or used as a grouping field
Bucketing is the right tool for a category every report and every user in the org should see consistently
questions.explain: Bucket columns are capped at five per report with twenty buckets each, and they live only inside the one report that defines them, with no new field or impact elsewhere. A value left out of every bucket just shows up under Unbucketed Values (and blank in the column) — it's not an error. Once created, a bucket column can be sorted, filtered, or grouped by like any other column. A category every report and user should see consistently calls for an actual custom or formula field, not a one-off bucket.

questions.prompt: An admin saves a new custom report type with Opportunity as the primary object, then later realizes the sales team actually needs Case as the primary object instead. What's the correct path forward?
options: Build a new custom report type from scratch with Case as the primary object — the primary object can't be changed once a custom report type is saved
Open the existing custom report type and change the primary object field, then click Save
Switch the report type's status to In Development, which unlocks the primary object field for editing
Change the primary object directly from Edit Layout, since that screen controls all of the type's core settings
questions.explain: The primary object is permanent the moment a custom report type is saved — it's the one setting from the setup wizard that can never be revisited. Fields, related objects, and layout can all be changed later, but a different primary object means building a new report type entirely.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a brand-new custom report type should be kept at status ________ while it's being tested, since that keeps it hidden from everyone except admins with Manage Custom Report Types permission.
questions.explain: In Development hides a custom report type from everyone except admins with the Manage Custom Report Types permission, which is exactly the testing window before it's ready for general use. Flipping it to Deployed is what finally makes it visible to report builders across the org.

questions.prompt: Match each report/dashboard folder access level to what it allows.
right: Full control, including the ability to re-share the folder with others
Run and edit the reports and dashboards saved inside the folder
Run reports in the folder, but can't edit or move them
questions.explain: Viewer can only run what's in the folder. Editor adds the ability to run and edit the reports and dashboards inside it. Manager is full control, including re-sharing the folder itself with other people — the most permissive of the three levels.

questions.prompt: What actually determines who can see a specific Salesforce report?
options: A sharing setting configured directly on the report record itself
The folder the report is saved in, and that folder's sharing settings
The report type the report was built from
The profile of whichever user originally created the report
Whether the report's format is Tabular, Summary, or Matrix
The object permissions on the report's primary object, independent of any folder
questions.explain: Reports have no sharing setting of their own. Visibility is controlled entirely by the folder a report is saved into and how that folder is shared — move the same report to a different folder and its audience changes immediately, with nothing else to touch.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A is the natural guess, since most Salesforce records do carry their own sharing settings — but reports are the exception. There is no sharing control on the report record itself; moving a report between folders is what actually changes who can see it, which is exactly the detail option A gets wrong.

questions.prompt: A VP wants a weekly pipeline report emailed to the whole sales team, but only on weeks when total pipeline value drops below target. Which two subscription settings together make this possible?
options: A weekly Schedule, combined with a Condition checking total pipeline against the target value
A weekly Schedule, combined with Run Report As set to the VP
Attach File set to Formatted Report, combined with a weekly Schedule
Edit Recipients set to the sales team's public group, with no other setting needed
questions.explain: Schedule controls when the subscription would normally fire — weekly, in this case. Conditions are what turn a routine delivery into a threshold-based alert: up to five conditions can be added, and the report only sends when every one is met, which is exactly "only send when pipeline drops below target."

questions.prompt: A finance analyst wants to pull a report's raw rows into a pivot table they maintain outside Salesforce. Select every true statement about exporting that's relevant here.
options: Details Only (.csv) gives flat, underlying records with no subtotals or grouping — the easiest shape to re-pivot elsewhere
Formatted Report (.xlsx) preserves groupings, subtotals, and the chart image, which is exactly the shape a pivot table needs
Encoding only needs attention when the exported data contains non-ASCII characters that come out garbled
If this export needs to happen every week, a subscription with Attach File turned on replaces the manual Export click
Export is only available for Tabular reports, never for grouped Summary or Matrix reports
questions.explain: Details Only gives flat rows with no subtotals or merged cells, which is far easier to re-pivot than a Formatted Report full of grouping and subtotal rows — the opposite of what the analyst needs. Encoding only matters when non-ASCII characters show up garbled. A recurring export belongs in a subscription with Attach File, not a standing manual habit. Export works the same way regardless of whether the report is Tabular, Summary, or Matrix.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a Case report with no date filter and no status filter is timing out for users. The single highest-leverage fix is filtering on something ________, rather than relying on "All Time" and "All Records."
questions.explain: An unfiltered or loosely filtered report over a large object forces the engine to scan every candidate record before it can group or summarize anything — the single most common cause of a report timing out. Filtering on something selective, like a date range or status, is the highest-leverage fix; adding a chart or an extra column does nothing to reduce the underlying scan.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: every number or chart on a dashboard is called a component or ________, and every single one is backed by a real report underneath it.
questions.explain: A dashboard stores no data of its own — it's a saved arrangement of widgets, each one pointing at a report, refreshed together whenever the dashboard runs. Change the underlying report and every widget using it updates automatically.

questions.prompt: A dashboard needs to show how many open Cases fall into each Priority tier, as a share of all open Cases. Which chart type fits, and why is a line chart the wrong choice?
options: Donut or pie, because it shows parts of a whole — a line chart implies a trend over time, which isn't what's being asked here
Line, because it's the most visually detailed chart type and detail is always preferable
Funnel, because Priority tiers always represent a sequence with expected drop-off, the same as a sales stage
Table, because case data should never be visualized, only listed
questions.explain: Donut and pie charts are built for parts-of-a-whole questions — exactly "what share of open cases is each priority tier." A line chart is for a trend over time, and Priority tiers aren't a time series, so a line chart would misrepresent the question entirely.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about dashboard filters, as distinct from report filters.
options: A dashboard filter is interactive and lets a viewer narrow the view in the moment, resetting each time they leave
A dashboard can have up to three filters, added through +Filter in the builder
Using a dashboard filter requires Editor or Manager access to the dashboard's folder
A report filter is baked into the report and applies the same way for every viewer, every time it runs
Adding a dashboard filter changes who is allowed to open the dashboard
questions.explain: Dashboard filters are interactive, viewer-facing, and reset on exit — up to three per dashboard, added via +Filter. A report filter, by contrast, is baked into the report itself and applies identically for every viewer. Using a filter needs no special access — any viewer who can already see the dashboard can use it — and it never changes who's allowed to open the dashboard in the first place; that's still controlled entirely by folder sharing.

questions.prompt: A sales VP wants one dashboard that every one of 40 reps can open and see only their own pipeline, without building 40 separate dashboards. What setting makes this possible, and why would a static dashboard fail?
options: A dynamic dashboard, where View Dashboard As is set to "the dashboard viewer" — a static dashboard always shows the same fixed running user's data to everyone, regardless of who's looking
A static dashboard with Run Report As set to Me on every underlying report
A dashboard filter on Opportunity Owner — static vs. dynamic has nothing to do with this scenario
Saving the dashboard in a private folder so each rep's session shows their own data automatically
questions.explain: A dynamic dashboard makes the running user whoever is currently viewing it, so the same single dashboard definition shows 40 different, accurate slices of data to 40 different reps. A static dashboard fixes one running user for everyone, which would show every rep that same person's data regardless of who's actually looking — and a dynamic dashboard specifically can't be saved in a private folder at all, since it needs to be viewable by more than one person.

questions.prompt: Match each dashboard widget type to the kind of thing it's built to show.
right: The raw rows themselves, when the detail is the point rather than a visual summary
A bar, line, donut, or funnel visualization of a grouped report
A single number, optionally measured against a target range
A single number shown on its own, with no target range
questions.explain: Chart covers bar, column, line, donut, and funnel visualizations of a grouped report. Metric is a single standalone number. Gauge is also a single number, but shown against a target range. Table is for when the raw underlying rows are what the viewer actually needs to see.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of adding a chart widget to a dashboard, per the Dashboard Components lesson, in the correct order.
items: Pick the source report the widget will visualize
Choose Display As — bar, column, line, donut, funnel, and so on
Set the Value being measured and what it's Sliced By
Review the live Preview, then add the widget to the dashboard
questions.explain: The Add Widget dialog always runs in this order: choose Chart, pick the report that already has the right grouping built in, pick a display type, set what's measured and sliced by, then check the live preview before committing — the widget never performs its own new calculation, it only visualizes what the source report already produces.

questions.prompt: A dashboard has twelve widgets, uses a different chart type for every similar question, and buries its most important number as the eighth thing a viewer sees. Select every design habit from the Dashboard Design Best Practices lesson that this dashboard violates.
options: Leading with what matters most, above the fold
Restraint over completeness
Consistency across widgets and dashboards
Sharing the dashboard's folder with the right audience
questions.explain: Burying the key number eighth violates leading with what matters most. Twelve widgets, when a handful of well-chosen ones would do, violates restraint over completeness. Using a different chart type for the same kind of question across widgets violates consistency. Nothing in the scenario says anything about who the folder is shared with, so that habit isn't implicated here.

questions.prompt: A pipeline-by-stage report shows healthy total pipeline value, but deals could still be stuck for months at one stage without that total ever reflecting it. Which report answers "what's at risk" that a pipeline-by-stage total alone can't?
options: A report filtered or sorted on Days in Current Stage, surfacing deals that have been stuck too long
The same pipeline-by-stage report, just re-run with a longer date range
A report of Closed Won opportunities only, since closed deals show the healthiest part of the pipeline
A report grouped by Opportunity Name instead of Stage, since names reveal which deals are stuck
questions.explain: Pipeline value alone hides exactly this problem — a deal stuck in Negotiation for 90 days looks identical, on a pipeline-by-stage total, to one that arrived yesterday. Reporting on Days in Current Stage is the early-warning report built specifically to surface stuck deals that a totals-only view can't show.

questions.prompt: Select every metric that support leaders actually track on a balanced service dashboard, per the Service Performance Reporting lesson.
options: Case volume — opened vs. closed, whether the queue is growing or shrinking
Case age — how long still-open cases have been sitting
Response and resolution time against an SLA or target
Customer satisfaction, when a post-case survey is in use
Pipeline coverage — total open pipeline against quota
questions.explain: Volume, age, response/resolution time, and satisfaction are the four numbers that dominate a balanced service dashboard. Pipeline coverage is a sales-pipeline concept from the previous lesson, not a support metric — Cases don't have a quota the way Opportunities do.

questions.prompt: Meridian's pipeline dashboard showed a healthy $4.2M against a $1M quota — more than 3x coverage — yet the team kept missing its number. Which report revealed the actual problem, and what was it?
options: A days-in-stage report, which showed 40% of that pipeline had been sitting in Proposal for over 60 days, well past the typical cycle time
A report of Closed Lost opportunities, which showed the team was simply losing too many deals
A report grouped by Lead Source, which showed most pipeline was coming from a weak source
The same pipeline dashboard, run more frequently, which would have caught the problem through repetition alone
questions.explain: The existing dashboard had only a total-pipeline widget, which hid the real issue entirely. A days-in-stage report (the same tool from the Sales Pipeline Reporting lesson) showed that 40% of the $4.2M had been stuck in Proposal for over 60 days against a normal 21-day cycle — the pipeline wasn't thin, it was stale, and total value alone couldn't reveal that.

questions.prompt: Meridian's Director of Support had an 18-hour average resolution time, comfortably under a 24-hour target, yet satisfaction kept slipping. The case study traced this to a small number of slow, complex warranty claims hidden inside one blended average. What specific report change fixed this without losing the overall trend?
options: Rebuilding the resolution-time report as a Matrix, grouped by Case Type in addition to the existing date grouping
Deleting the warranty claim cases from the report so the average only reflects fast cases
Switching the report from a Summary to a Tabular format so every individual case is listed
Lowering the SLA target from 24 hours to 18 hours to match the current average
questions.explain: The 18-hour blended average hid a small number of 4-5 day warranty claims behind a large volume of fast, simple cases. Rebuilding the report as a Matrix grouped by Case Type split "Account Admin" (fast, high-volume) from "Warranty Claim" (slow, high-impact) instead of blending them, while still keeping the date grouping for the overall trend.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: before calling a dashboard build finished, the Practice Lab says to ________ it against the design checklist from the Dashboard Design Best Practices lesson.
questions.explain: The lab's closing step is a deliberate self-review pass against the Lesson 18 checklist — does the key number load above the fold, could any widget be cut, are titles descriptive, is the folder shared correctly — rather than treating the build as done the moment it's assembled.

questions.prompt: A second sales manager wants the exact same Sales Pipeline Overview dashboard, but scoped to their own, different team, without building a second dashboard from scratch. Select the two features that make this possible.
options: A dynamic dashboard, so the running user (and their data access) is whoever is viewing it
A dashboard filter, such as one on Owner, so each manager can narrow the shared dashboard to their own team
A brand-new custom report type built specifically for the second manager's team
Exporting the first manager's dashboard as a CSV and re-importing it under a new name
questions.explain: A dynamic dashboard makes the running user whoever's currently viewing it, so each manager's data access applies automatically from the same single definition. A dashboard filter on a shared field like Owner then lets each manager narrow the view to just their own team's deals. Neither a new report type nor an export/re-import gets at the real need — one dashboard definition serving multiple audiences.
